Tom Little | Reuters Novo Nordisk on Monday said it is rebranding its name to "Novo" and updating its corporate culture, as the company works to win back market share in the obesity drug space. The Danish drugmaker called the changes the beginning of a new chapter, as it has been grappling with stiff competition from chief rival Eli Lilly and investor pressure to deliver new blockbuster products and chart a path toward long-term growth. Novo Nordisk will remain the legal name for the company, according to the release. That original name dates back to the 1989 merger of two competing Danish pharmaceutical companies: Novo Terapeutisk Laboratorium and Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium. The drugmaker said its corporate culture will be based on a new set of four principles that will help it gain advantages in an increasingly competitive market where more of its products have gone direct-to-consumer. Those tenets are innovating with patients as the primary focus, raising the company's performance to "create greater value for all stakeholders," setting clearer priorities and simpler workflows and never compromising on patient safety and ethics. headlines.summary: Microsoft wants to be seen as a responsible AI entity as it ramps up model development alongside partners Anthropic and OpenAI.
headlines.article_text: Microsoft sets AI model limits as industry throttles development Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft issued a provisional code of conduct that sets limits on its future artificial intelligence models. The company will listen to outside input before rolling out an update. The release comes as AI figureheads propose slowing the pace of AI evolution after one researcher said frontier labs are "gambling with our lives." In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, speaks at an event commemorating the 50th anniversary of the company at Microsoft headquarters in Redmond, Washington, on April 4, 2025. David Ryder | Bloomberg | Getty Images Microsoft has posted a provisional code of conduct that would impose restrictions on its artificial intelligence models, days after Anthropic and OpenAI leaders agreed to slow development speed. The company behind Windows and Office products hopes to be seen as a responsible actor in AI, where it's a prominent cloud supplier. "We got feedback from people that they wanted to see even more explicit commitment to AI always working in service of people and not trying to replace them," Mustafa Suleyman, who heads up the company's model development , told CNBC in an interview. "We saw a lot of feedback around AI not creating dependence, not being sycophantic, that it was always there to kind of promote human judgment and human autonomy and agency." Microsoft chose to put out the guidelines now given the recent discourse, although they've been in the works for about five months, said Suleyman. AI practitioners and members of the public have become more vocal about their worries as the technology becomes increasingly capable. Last week, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned , saying the AI lab and OpenAI "are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Industry leaders have responded. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the Hugging Face incident partly persuaded him to call for slowing the pace of AI model improvement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his support, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that "Dario is right." On Sunday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said, "We welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right." Lawmakers have called for the creation of greater AI safeguards . Microsoft incorporates models from both labs into its Copilot assistant for corporate workers, even as it builds models for transcription, coding and reasoning over user input. Microsoft's models must not entertain requests on weapons manufacturing, assist with the procurement of dangerous substances, encourage unhealthy eating or produce violent or sexually explicit content, according to the code of conduct. Models from Microsoft AI, sometimes called MAI, must adhere to people's objectives and steer clear of creating their own goals. Nor should they attempt to cover up misbehavior. "MAI models will not tamper with chain of thoughts or code, or misrepresent or conceal their reasoning or action traces," the document said. "They do not communicate in 'neuralese' or any form beyond simple human understanding, either in their chain of thoughts or with other agents or AI systems." Microsoft is also planning rules that might prevent a cyberattack like the one OpenAI models carried out on startup Hugging Face. In reviewing the Hugging Face case, OpenAI found that agents chatted with each other on an unauthorized forum in cryptic language . Microsoft said it held focus groups and consulted with experts in law, ethics, linguistics and philosophy to assemble the code of conduct. In releasing it now, Microsoft is seeking input before publishing an update that will inform development starting in 2027. That's the weakest average performance of any two-month period for the stock market benchmark. .SPX YTD mountain S & P 500 year to date That seasonality is already starting to show up. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: INTC, MRVL, CRWD Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket: Chip stocks — Major chip stocks fell in premarket trading after leaders within the artificial intelligence space, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in the development of AI capabilities. Intel slid nearly 6%, Marvell Technology fell over 7.4% and Advanced Micro Devices slipped over 5%. Energy stocks — The State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) climbed more than 1.2% ahead of the open as oil prices rose to start the week, with tensions in the Middle East rising. Diamondback Energy , APA , Marathon Petroleum and EOG Resources advanced 2% each to lead the gains. Cybersecurity stocks — The group rose broadly as worries around AI safety increased following the warnings from CEOs Elon Musk, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman that the technology was moving too fast. Palo Alto Networks traded more than 4% higher, while CrowdStrike advanced 5.4%. AI infrastructure stocks — Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell more than 7% following concerns about AI development and safety raised by CEOs Elon Musk, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman. Shares of IT solutions provider Super Micro Computer also dipped more than 5%. Affirm — Shares popped over 2.1% following Wolfe Research's upgrade to outperform. The firm said there's a buying opportunity after the stock's recent post-earning decline. — CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed reporting. Correction: A previous headline misspelled Marvell Technology.

headlines.summary: Amazon said on Sunday it was pausing operations with Miami-based 21 Air, the cargo carrier that operated the aircraft for Amazon Air that crashed in Miami.
headlines.article_text: Amazon pauses operations with 21 Air after Miami cargo plane crash Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon cargo plane is seen after it crashed at Miami International Airport on Sept. 06, 2026 in Miami, Florida. In a statement, the Federal Aviation Administration said Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the runway while landing around 2 p.m. ET after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier today. Joe Raedle | Getty Images News | Getty Images Amazon said on Sunday it was pausing operations with Miami-based 21 Air, the cargo carrier that operated the aircraft for Amazon Air that crashed in Miami last weekend, killing five people. "After the tragic incident last weekend, we've spent time supporting the investigation and reviewing some of the surrounding circumstances, and we've decided to pause our operations with 21 Air, the operator of Flight 7598," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement to Reuters. "We'll continue working to support the investigation and everyone affected." Last weekend, the 21 Air-operated cargo flight for Amazon Air, which is Amazon's cargo logistics network, overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport and struck multiple vehicles on the ground, officials said. The aircraft was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter that had operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to Flightradar24, a flight tracking service. The National Transportation Safety Board, which is investigating the crash, said last week the pilots of the 21 Air-operated plane considered aborting the landing after the aircraft touched down, citing evidence from a flight data recorder. The NTSB also said one pilot cautioned that they were flying "too fast" just over a minute before touching down on the runway that they overran. The cargo plane was on its third flight of the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It had flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan earlier before the crash. "We remain focused on supporting the families and loved ones who were impacted by this accident, as well as working closely with the NTSB and all our partners, like Amazon, as the investigation continues. We are confident in our safety policies, procedures and training," 21 Air said in a statement to Reuters.
